articles.body: 1. Problem and background This installment of the paper deep-read series takes a plant phenotyping / agricultural counting paper from the last three months and checks its evaluation protocol against three questions fixed in advance: does it match predictions to ground truth instance by instance, does it report results per category, and does it include quantitative stress tests for occlusion and illumination? The paper is Chili-Seg (Kuang et al., Frontiers in Plant Science 17:1955273, published 29 September 2026, doi:10.3389/fpls.2026.1955273), a chili-flower instance segmentation model built on YOLO11n-seg. It explicitly targets small objects, leaf occlusion, and variable illumination, and it names flower counting and robotic pollination as downstream uses.

articles.title: OpenAI's Pretraining Loss Is Falling 7x Faster — and the Benchmarks Haven't Noticed Yet
articles.excerpt: OpenAI just did something no frontier lab had done before: it published the pretraining loss of every model it has trained since GPT-3.5 — thirteen models, measured on one fixed held-out dataset drawn…
articles.body: OpenAI just did something no frontier lab had done before: it published the pretraining loss of every model it has trained since GPT-3.5 — thirteen models, measured on one fixed held-out dataset drawn from its own codebase. And the curve it released does not look like the slow, grinding progress scaling laws promised. It looks like a bend in the road. METR ran the numbers, and the result is startling. The numbers From 2022 through early 2026, OpenAI's base-model log-perplexity fell slowly, about 0.022 per year . Then, at a breakpoint in February 2026 , the slope changed. Since then it has been falling at about 0.156 per year — 7.1 times steeper .

articles.title: On this day in space! Nov. 24, 1947: The US Navy launches the 1st Aerobee sounding rocket, but it didn't reach space
articles.excerpt: On Nov. 24, 1947, the U.S. Navy launched the first Aerobee rocket into the sky, but it never reached space. Here's why it mattered.
articles.body: On Nov. 24, 1947, the U.S. Navy launched the first Aerobee rocket into the sky, but it never reached space. Aerobee was a suborbital sounding rocket designed to study Earth's atmosphere . After World War 2, the United States started reusing erman V-2 rockets for this kind of research. When they started running out of V-2 rockets , the United States constructed its own rockets that were similar but cheaper to build and to launch. In the weeks leading up to the first Aerobee mission, three test flights were launched. Those tests used a dummy version of Aerobee with a live booster to see if the two stages would separate properly. On Aerobee's first real flight, the rocket flew about 35 miles high. That's below the 62-mile (100 kilometers) upper limit for the boundary of space .

The new show casts replicants as the dominant species on Earth, with humans relegated to second-class citizens after a global uprising. This dreary dystopian cyberpunk realm originates from sci-fi legend Phillip K. Dick's 1968 novel, "Do Androids Dream of Electric Sheep?," and was then so vividly brought to life in Ridley Scott’s seminal 1982 adaptation, " Blade Runner ." The 2017 sequel, "Blade Runner 2049," was directed by "Arrival’s" and "Dune’s" Denis Villeneuve.

articles.title: Amateur Astronomer? Be a Kilonova Catcher!
articles.excerpt: Neutron stars are the ultra-dense, city-sized leftovers of dead stars. When they collide, they can release a brief flash of light called a kilonova. These immensely powerful events forge much of the u…
articles.body: Explore This Section Science Citizen Science Amateur Astronomer? Be a… Overview Resources Opportunities Citizen Science Highlights About Science Activation Neutron stars are the ultra-dense, city-sized leftovers of dead stars. When they collide, they can release a brief flash of light called a kilonova . These immensely powerful events forge much of the universe’s gold, platinum and other heavy elements. Since a kilonova fades within days, astronomers have to find it fast, and no single observatory can watch the whole sky. But if you have a telescope with a camera, or access to one, you can help find and follow these cosmic fireworks as a part of NASA’s Kilonova Catcher project! Kilonova Catcher connects amateur astronomers around the world into a rapid-response network.
